searches.note: The two shared searches read the Chablis and Bourgogne wine bodies on the decree of 1938, the seven climats in order and the district's history (the Paris trade, Pontigny, phylloxera, the frosts of 1945 and 1957, the recovery). WebFetch was not tried. Thirty five searches of the share are left unspent.

method: The fragment was written and first refuted with little or no search (the author's searches ran out after Raveneau and Dauvissat; the first refuter had none); this recheck searched every fact beyond the Codex, strongest first: the founding years and the people, the classification and the decree, the sites, the making and its months, the label words and each beat of the story.

Every source address the fragment listed was tested; where no search returned it (the Vintus page, SommSelect, the reference books), it was replaced by a page a search did return. Every source is read: search, from the body's own domain where marked primary (the Chablis wine body, the Bourgogne wine body, La Chablisienne, Bouchard, the Fèvre sheet in its owners' directory).

A fact in two independent sources or one primary stands; a fact in one secondary only, or nowhere, is softened or taken out and listed here. A writer's own site (Inside Burgundy, a writer's wiki, a critic's blog) was read as a lead and never cited.

The rules were tried on every string: no living person named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash; the questions for one right answer, plausible distractors and an explanation that teaches.

tested: The founding of 1948 by marriage into the Dauvissat family, the vines bought and the wife's family's plots joined (Wikipedia, Vins et Millésimes, Decanter's Raveneau profile): confirmed.

The first bottling at the domaine, from the 1960s, the first of the family to bottle (Wikipedia and a second account): confirmed; the record's earlier generations who sold their grapes: one account says the father had sold vineyards, so it is rephrased.
The grand cru purchases in Les Clos, Valmur and Blanchot through the 1960s and 1970s (Wikipedia, Vins et Millésimes, Fine and Rare): confirmed.
The sons: one joined in 1978, the other in 1995 (two accounts for 1978); the founder's retirement is 1988 or 1995 and his death 2000 in one account; his birth year found nowhere.

The making: steel tank, then used feuillettes of 132 litres, a year to eighteen months (Rare Wine Co, Sommelier Academy, Inside Burgundy): confirmed; one merchant's barrel fermentation is the outlier.

Les Clos the largest climat, south west facing, stony above and clay below, named for its dry stone walls, possibly the Pontigny monks' first kernel; the Paris trade by the Yonne; the decree of 1938 and the seven climats in order (the Chablis and Bourgogne wine bodies' own pages): confirmed.
The label wording François Raveneau: one search, no label text found.

The rules: nobody living named (the sons are not), no price, no score, nothing volatile (the parcel sizes stay out), no judging superlative, no bare family word, British, no dash; the two questions have one key each and distractors of one kind, and each explanation names the nearest wrong option: sound.

changed.was: Chablis grew rich in the Middle Ages on wine shipped down the Yonne to Paris, and the story goes that Les Clos was among the first slopes worked by the Cistercian monks of Pontigny, an abbey founded in 1114; its name recalls the dry stone walls that once enclosed the vines. Frost, phylloxera and war shrank the vineyard, and in 1938 the law gave the hill's seven climats a single appellation, Chablis Grand Cru. Ten years later François Raveneau, who died in 2000, married into the Dauvissat family and joined his vines to theirs. Earlier generations had sold their grapes; he was the first of the family to bottle wine under its own name. Through the 1960s and 1970s, as grand cru land came up for sale, he bought parcels in Les Clos, Valmur and Blanchot. His two sons worked beside him for years before they took charge, and they kept his method: fermentation in tank, then a year and more in old casks. In their cellar Les Clos shows that Chablis can be raised in wood and keep the taste of its limestone. On a list it belongs with the wines to cellar, not with the crisp aperitifs.
changed.now: Chablis grew rich in the Middle Ages on wine shipped down the Yonne to Paris, and the Cistercian monks of Pontigny worked its slopes from the twelfth century; Les Clos may be the first kernel of their vineyard, and its name recalls the dry stone walls that once enclosed the vines. Phylloxera, war and frost shrank the district, and in 1938 the law gave the hill's seven climats a single appellation, Chablis Grand Cru. Ten years later the founder, whose name the domaine carries, married into the Dauvissat family, and the vines he had bought and the plots his wife's family held became one domaine. He was the first of his family to bottle his own wine, from the 1960s, and through the 1960s and 1970s, as grand cru land came up for sale, he bought parcels in Les Clos, Valmur and Blanchot. One son joined him in 1978 and a second followed, and they kept his method: fermentation in tank, then a year and more in old casks. In their cellar Les Clos shows that Chablis can be raised in wood and keep the taste of its limestone. On a list it belongs with the wines to cellar, not with the crisp aperitifs.
changed.why: The founder's dates are not in two sources, so he is described; Pontigny's founding year was not searched; the bottling from the 1960s and the sons' arrival are as Wikipedia and Vins et Millésimes give them; the Pontigny kernel is hedged as the wine body hedges it.

changed.was: Bottling at the domaine was rare in Chablis in 1931, when most growers sold their wine in cask to the merchants, but that year the founder of this estate, built up through the 1920s, began to bottle his own. In 1938 Chablis Grand Cru became an appellation, and the seven climats of the hill took one name on the label with their own beneath it. The founder's son widened the holdings from the 1950s, and the family became kin by marriage to the Raveneaus, so the two domaines that would be named together grew up side by side. The founder's grandson joined in the 1970s and took charge in 1989. He kept the cellar as he found it: old barrels, the small Chablis feuillette, long lees ageing and no taste of new oak, and in the early 2000s he turned the vineyards to organic farming. Les Preuses and Les Clos are the domaine's two grands crus, the first rounder and more open, the second firmer and slower. When a guest asks for Chablis raised in wood that keeps the taste of its limestone, Dauvissat is the other name beside Raveneau, and Les Preuses is the easier of its grands crus to open young.
changed.now: Few Chablis growers bottled their own wine in 1931, when most sold it in cask to the merchants, but that year the founder of this domaine became one of the first to do so. In 1938 Chablis Grand Cru became an appellation, and the seven climats of the hill took one name on the label with their own beneath it. The founder's son was at work in the domaine from 1950, and his sister's marriage to the founder of Raveneau made the two families kin, so the domaines named together grew up side by side. The founder's grandson joined his father in 1976 and in time took charge. He kept the cellar as he found it: old barrels, the small Chablis feuillette, long lees ageing and little or no new oak, and in the early 2000s he turned the vineyards to organic farming. Les Preuses and Les Clos are the domaine's two grands crus, the first rounder and more open, the second firmer and slower. When a guest asks for Chablis raised in wood that keeps the taste of its limestone, Dauvissat is the other name beside Raveneau, and Les Preuses is the easier of its grands crus to open young.
changed.why: Decanter dates the son's start to 1950 and the grandson's arrival to 1976, and gives the takeover as 1979 where two lesser accounts say 1989; the 1920s rest on one account; the kinship is the son's sister's marriage, as both Decanter profiles tell it; organic from 2002 is in two accounts.

changed.was: When the law drew the Chablis appellations in 1938, it gave the seven climats of the hill above the Serein one name, Chablis Grand Cru, but the district it named was in decline: frost, phylloxera and war had left only a fraction of its old vineyard planted. The domaine was founded in 1959, on the eve of the district's recovery, and over the decades that followed its founder gathered parcels in Les Clos, Bougros, Les Preuses, Valmur and Vaudésir until it held one of the largest shares of grand cru in the district. For years its wines were known for new oak, which divided opinion in a place that prizes the taste of its limestone. In 1998 the domaine was sold to the Henriot family of Champagne, who had bought Bouchard Père et Fils in Beaune three years earlier, in 1995. The new owners turned the cellar away from new barrels and raised the grands crus partly in steel and partly in older oak. Côte Bouguerots is the steep part of Bougros, and the house bottles it under its own name, so that a guest can taste one slope within a climat. Here a large domaine's grand cru tastes of the hill, not of the cellar.
changed.now: When the law drew the Chablis appellations in 1938, it gave the seven climats of the hill above the Serein one name, Chablis Grand Cru, but the district was in decline: phylloxera, war and frost had left only a fraction of its old vineyard planted, and the frost of 1957 took a whole crop. The domaine was founded in 1959 as the Domaine de la Maladière, by a grower whose family had long worked vines in Chablis, on the eve of the district's recovery, and over the decades that followed it came to hold one of the largest shares of grand cru in the district, in Les Clos, Bougros, Les Preuses, Valmur and Vaudésir. Its founder favoured new oak, which divided opinion in a place that prizes the taste of its limestone. In 1998 the domaine passed to the Henriot family of Champagne, who had taken the helm of Bouchard Père et Fils in Beaune in 1995. The new team set the new barrels aside and raised the grands crus in steel and older oak. Côte Bouguerots is the steep lower slope of Bougros, and the house bottles it under its own name, so that a guest can taste one slope within a climat. Here a large domaine's grand cru tastes of the hill, not of the cellar.
changed.why: Founded as the Domaine de la Maladière; the frost of 1957 by the wine body; the founder's new oak; the domaine, not certainly its vineyards, passed in 1998; Bouchard in 1995 by its own page.

changed.was: The domaine counts its beginnings from 1850, when Chablis was a busy vineyard sending its wine to Paris in cask, much of it in the small local barrel, the feuillette. The decades that followed were hard on it: phylloxera, two wars and the spring frosts left only a fraction of the old vineyard standing, and when the law drew its appellations in 1938 the district was at a low ebb. Recovery came after the 1960s, when sprinklers and heaters against frost let growers plant again, and through it the Michel family took the opposite road from the old barrel domaines. In the second half of the twentieth century they gave up oak altogether, and every wine of the house, grand cru included, has since been fermented and aged in stainless steel. Their argument is that Chablis needs nothing from wood: the cold climate and the Kimmeridgian marl give the acidity, the salt and the shell, and steel keeps them clear. Montée de Tonnerre, the premier cru that carries on from the grand cru hill, is where that argument is heard at its fullest. Poured beside a Raveneau or a Dauvissat from the same ground, it shows a guest what the cellar changes and what the vineyard does not.
changed.now: The family counts its beginnings from 1850, when it planted its first vines in Chablis, then a busy vineyard sending its wine to Paris by river. The decades that followed were hard: phylloxera, wars and spring frosts left only a fraction of the old vineyard standing, and when the law drew its appellations in 1938 the district was at a low ebb. Recovery came after the frost of 1957, when heaters and sprinklers let growers plant again, and through it the Michel family took the opposite road from the old barrel domaines. Until then their wines had been made in old oak; from the end of the 1960s they turned to steel, and by about 1980 the last barrels were gone, so that every wine of the house, grand cru included, is fermented and aged in stainless steel. Their argument is that Chablis needs nothing from wood: the cold climate and the Kimmeridgian marl give the acidity, the salt and the shell, and steel keeps them clear. Montée de Tonnerre, the premier cru across from the grand cru hill, is where that argument is heard at its fullest. Poured beside a Raveneau or a Dauvissat from the same ground, it shows a guest what the cellar changes and what the vineyard does not.
changed.why: The change to steel began with the vintages at the end of the 1960s and was complete by about 1980; the recovery followed the frost of 1957, by the wine body.

changed.was: After the First World War Chablis was a shrunken vineyard: phylloxera had taken most of its vines, and its growers sold their grapes and wine to the merchants. In 1923 a group of them joined together to make and sell their wine as one, and La Chablisienne was born. Fifteen years later, in 1938, the law gave the seven climats of the grand cru hill a single appellation, Chablis Grand Cru. The cooperative grew with the district's recovery after the 1960s, when protection against spring frost let the vineyard spread again, until its members farmed a large share of the appellation. Grenouilles is the smallest of the seven climats, set between Vaudésir and Valmur; its name means frogs, which, the story goes, once sang from the banks of the Serein below. Most of it came to belong to Château Grenouilles, an estate whose vines the cooperative works and whose wine it bottles apart under the château's name. That a grand cru should come from a cooperative surprises many guests, and it is a question the Court asks. Château Grenouilles is the proof that Chablis Grand Cru is not the wine of small domaines alone.
changed.now: In the hard years after the First World War, when Chablis wine was difficult to sell, a group of growers led by a priest joined together in 1923 to make and sell their wine as one, and La Chablisienne was born. Fifteen years later, in 1938, the law gave the seven climats of the grand cru hill a single appellation, Chablis Grand Cru. The cooperative grew with the district's recovery after the frosts of the 1950s, until its members farmed a large share of the appellation. Grenouilles is the smallest of the seven climats, set between Vaudésir and Valmur beside the Serein; its name, written as early as 1321, means frogs. Most of it lies in one block, Château Grenouilles, an estate the cooperative took on in 2003, by its own account, and whose wine it bottles apart under the château's name. That a grand cru should come from a cooperative surprises many guests, and it is a question a candidate meets. Château Grenouilles is the proof that Chablis Grand Cru is not the wine of small domaines alone.
changed.why: The cooperative's own page gives the founding under a priest in hard years and the château held since 2003; the wine body gives the name's first record in 1321.
